messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Gerald is a 58-year-old dentist of Canadian descent, currently living with his long-term partner in a mid-sized American city. He was referred for psychological assessment following a significant decline in his professional functioning and a near-complete withdrawal from social life. His PCL-5 score of 77 places him in the severe range, and what emerges across the intake and early sessions is a man whose world has contracted almost beyond recognition since an encounter with police approximately fourteen months ago.

Gerald had been driving home from an evening continuing education seminar when he was pulled over in an unfamiliar neighbourhood. What began as a routine stop escalated within seconds: he was ordered out of the vehicle at gunpoint, forced face-down onto the asphalt, and held there — a knee pressed into the centre of his back — for what he estimates was close to eight minutes. He remembers the sound of radio static and shouted commands, and the specific sensation of gravel cutting into his cheek. No charges were ever filed. No apology was offered. The officers involved were not disciplined. Gerald drove himself home that night and told no one for three weeks.

The memory of the event has a quality he struggles to articulate — he describes it as feeling like it happened to someone else, a kind of footage from another person's life that nonetheless arrives with full sensory force. When it surfaces, he hears the radio static again, and he feels the pressure and pain across his upper back and ribs as though the weight has never fully lifted. These intrusive returns are not neutral. Each time the memory floods back, Gerald finds himself arriving at the same dark conclusion: that there must be something about him — some quality others can read — that invited what happened. He cannot fully articulate what that quality is, but the certainty that it exists has settled into him like a belief he never consciously chose. The memory does not simply replay; it prosecutes him. And because the prosecution never ends, he has come to feel that his life as he knew it has been destroyed — that the person who drove to that seminar no longer exists, and that nothing adequate has been done to account for what was taken from him.

The sense of injustice and self-blame that the memory generates feeds back into how he holds the memory itself: he ruminates on it, turns it over, searching for the moment he could have prevented it, and in doing so keeps the event perpetually present and unresolved. When the memory arrives, it also arrives as threat — the world it conjures is one in which danger comes without warning, from figures of authority, from strangers, from any situation he cannot fully control. He now feels threatened by strangers approaching him in ordinary situations, including, with increasing frequency, patients entering his operatory. He has begun positioning himself in his dental chair so that he always has a clear sightline to the door, and he scans the waiting room when he passes through it in a way his receptionist has quietly noticed.

The threat he carries with him has reshaped his behaviour across months. He avoids anything he anticipates might be stressful — he has declined two professional conferences, stopped attending his partner's family gatherings, and reduced his patient load by nearly a third. More broadly, he avoids any emotional activation at all, positive or negative, as though feeling anything risks opening a door he cannot close. He no longer watches films, avoids music he once loved, and has described meals with his partner as something he endures rather than enjoys. This emotional blunting has not protected him; instead, the avoidance has kept him from processing what happened, and the memory remains as raw as it was in the early weeks. The strategies that were meant to contain his distress have quietly confirmed his belief that he is permanently damaged — that a man who must manage his life so carefully must have something fundamentally wrong with him.

What finally brought Gerald to seek help was his partner's direct statement that she no longer recognised him. He arrives at sessions sitting with his back to the wall, watching the door. What he most fears is that the clinician will confirm what he already suspects. What he most hopes — though he says it with little conviction — is that he is wrong.
